clue.text: Court cast man out after one produces very good deeds (13, two words)

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come after the single letter, so that letter leads the answer

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article

indicators.note: letters put out of their places are disordered, so these words get rearranged

parts.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A court has banished a man, and somehow this counts as doing good.
explanation.walkthrough: ACTA SANCTORUM is Latin for 'deeds of the saints', the great collection of saints' lives compiled by the Bollandists.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin title literally means the acts of holy people, so saintly good works are what it records.

clue.text: Chef after removing tail brought round hot salmon

indicators.note: something brought round another thing encircles it, so the shortened word wraps the abbreviation
taking off the tail means the last letter of the word for chef goes

parts.note: a chef is a cook
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A chef serves up a salmon dish piping hot.
explanation.walkthrough: COOK loses its K to leave COO, and H goes inside: CO-H-O.
explanation.definitionFit: The coho is a Pacific salmon species, also called the silver salmon.

clue.text: Patterned lace forming lines tyro spins round

indicators.note: the rearranged word goes round the other piece, enclosing it
a word that spins gets its letters whirled into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A beginner at lacemaking twirls the bobbins and a pattern of lines appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spins round' looks like one phrase, but it does two jobs: spins rearranges and round encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: Trolly is a kind of bobbin lace whose pattern is outlined with a thicker thread, a specialist term in Chambers.

clue.text: Estates of a kind, special, landed with time in a bundle (11, two words)

indicators.note: the time letter sits in the bundle word, placed inside it

parts.note: SP is an abbreviation for special
lit is a past tense of light, to land or alight
a truss is a bundle, as of hay
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A special estate has landed with time bundled up in it, like a legal parcel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landed' sounds like landed property, matching estates, but it means alighted.
explanation.definitionFit: Split trusts are trust arrangements dividing a property between income and capital beneficiaries, so they are a type of legal estate.

clue.text: Tough apparently, and long

parts.note: the opening of the word, used as a shortening of it
to long for something is to ache for it

explanation.surface: Someone seems hard and lanky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough' is a noun here: an apache is a Parisian street thug. The AP for 'apparently' is not a standard abbreviation, so this part of the parse is uncertain.
explanation.definitionFit: An apache was a violent ruffian of early twentieth-century Paris, a tough in the noun sense.

clue.text: Molluscs? There's adult out in lake swimming with purpose

indicators.note: letters that swim about move freely and settle in a new order

parts.note: A was the film certificate for adult audiences
taken as written for rearranging
L is the map abbreviation for lake
an idea is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: A grown-up goes swimming in a lake with some purpose in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out in' looks like ordinary surface glue, but those two words are part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Nautiloidea is the zoological group of shelled cephalopods including the nautilus; the question mark flags a group name rather than a plain noun.

clue.text: Gossip from Dublin or circa (roughly)

indicators.note: done roughly means not done precisely, so the letters land out of order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Dublin chatter, or something like it, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circa (roughly)' reads as a gloss, circa meaning about; but roughly is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Craic is the Irish word for fun, banter and lively talk, so Dublin chat or news fits.

clue.text: Practise mind-reading? These leap out with it

indicators.note: words knocked out of shape are rearranged into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether mind-reading is being practised as these thoughts leap out.
explanation.definitionFit: To telepathise is to communicate thought directly to another mind, a fair description of mind-reading.

clue.text: What's left of joint cut short?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the butt end of a cannabis cigarette
second meaning: to clip a horse's mane short

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one question about a joint of meat trimmed down; the two halves are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Roach is slang for a smoked joint's stub, and as a verb means to trim hair or a mane close.

clue.text: Cheerful maestro lifts his stick for this

definitions.meaning: first meaning: optimistic, in good spirits

definitions.text: maestro lifts his stick for this
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the unaccented beat a conductor marks with a rising baton

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a cryptic description: the conductor's stick goes up on this beat, just before the bar line.
explanation.definitionFit: Upbeat means optimistic, and in music it names the unstressed beat marked by an upward stroke of the baton.

clue.text: To marry girl 'e'll display jacquard material

parts.note: to mate is to pair or marry
a lass is a girl
the dropped-aitch he leaves just E

explanation.surface: A cockney suitor promises to wed his girl and show off a fine fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'e marks the dropped H of he, leaving E.
explanation.definitionFit: Matelassé is a fabric woven on a jacquard loom with a raised, quilted-looking pattern.

clue.text: Wild Irish robber getting cut in loot

indicators.note: the cutting word is placed in the loot word, inside it

parts.note: rape in its old sense is plunder or loot
to pare is to cut or trim

explanation.surface: An Irish bandit takes his cut of the spoils.
explanation.walkthrough: Rape here is the archaic word for plunder, not the modern crime.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapparee was a seventeenth-century Irish irregular soldier or freebooter, so an outlaw robber.

clue.text: Being shy, one constant in make-believe, hiding head

indicators.note: the pair of letters goes in the shortened make-believe word
hiding its head means the word's first letter is concealed and dropped

parts.note: pretence is make-believe
I is the Roman numeral one
c is the symbol for a constant, as the speed of light

explanation.surface: A shy person keeps up a steady pretence and hides their face.
explanation.walkthrough: The make-believe word loses its first letter before the other two letters go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Reticence is reserve or reluctance to speak, the state of being shy.

clue.text: Cry from anonymous boat?

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for anonymous
a hoy is a small coasting vessel or barge

explanation.surface: Someone shouts from a boat with no name on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoy is a crossword staple for a small sailing barge.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahoy is the sailor's call used to hail another vessel, so a shout or cry.

clue.text: Some dub a beauty this

indicators.note: some of the following words means only part of their letters is taken

parts.note: the run of letters across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: Some people would call a good-looking person by this name.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a babe is what some people call a beauty, and 'dub' is to name.
explanation.definitionFit: Babe is slang for an attractive person, a term some people use to address or describe a beauty.

clue.text: Acid that ruins coutil

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so the word's letters fall into a new arrangement

parts.note: coutil is a tough twilled cotton used for corsets; these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A corrosive acid spoils a piece of corset fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Toluic acid is a methylbenzoic acid derived from toluene, so it names a specific acid.

clue.text: Falconer's charge, one held in three lines

indicators.note: something held in another is gripped inside it, so the numeral goes within

parts.note: a variant spelling of tercel, the male hawk a falconer keeps
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A falconer looks after one bird across three lines of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes into TERCET after its T; tercet is also three rhyming lines, the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiercet is a variant of tercet, a group of three lines of verse rhyming together.

clue.text: Badly hit in outbreak of E. coli, very early

indicators.note: one jumbled group sits in the other
badly done means jumbled, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: the bacterium name, letters only

indicators.note: an outbreak scatters things, so the letters of the bacterium burst into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is badly hit by an E. coli outbreak early on.
explanation.definitionFit: Eolithic refers to the earliest stage of the Stone Age, marked by crude flint tools, so extremely early in prehistory.

clue.text: Carmen, say, individual life-force around opera's denouement

indicators.note: the life-force word goes around the single letter

parts.note: chi or qi is the vital energy in each person in Chinese thought

indicators.note: the denouement is the end of a story, so only the word's final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of opera

explanation.surface: Carmen, a single lively force of nature, dominates the opera's ending.
explanation.walkthrough: Carmen in Bizet's opera is a Romani woman; chai is a Romani word for a woman of that people.
explanation.definitionFit: Chai is a Romani word for a Romani woman or girl, and Carmen is the most famous fictional example.

clue.text: Period after work for high achiever in maths (Cantab)

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other, fixing their order in the answer

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
a period is a time

explanation.surface: A spell of time after study goes to a Cambridge maths star.
explanation.walkthrough: Cantab means of Cambridge University.
explanation.definitionFit: At Cambridge, an optime is a student placed in the second or third class of the Mathematical Tripos, below the wranglers.

clue.text: Brilliant performer topping bill, taking wing with luminance

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it, so the performer word encloses the rest

parts.note: the star is the headline act at the top of a bill
el is a wing or extension built at right angles to a building
L is the symbol for luminance

explanation.surface: A headline act takes flight with a dazzling glow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wing' suggests flight, but it is the architectural kind: an extension of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: Stellar means outstanding or star-like, a common sense of brilliant.

clue.text: Musician as once found in catalogue

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so the short word sits within

parts.note: a list is a catalogue
ut is Latin for as, the language once spoken

explanation.surface: A musician turns up in a catalogue, as used to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: A lutist is a player of the lute, so a kind of musician.

clue.text: Extract from flamenco recording — it rarely features in programme

indicators.note: an extract is a piece taken out of something larger, here a run of letters

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A clip from a flamenco recording that seldom appears on a concert bill.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is fair because an encore is an extra piece not listed in the printed programme.
explanation.definitionFit: An encore is an unannounced extra performance demanded by the audience, so it is rarely printed in the concert programme.

clue.text: Choir's niche filling the space from the east

indicators.note: in an across entry, reading from the east means right to left
a filling sits inside, so the letters come from within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A choir's recess fills the eastern part of the building.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits a church nicely, since the apse is usually at the east end.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a vaulted semicircular recess, often at the east end of a church beyond the choir.

clue.text: One's found among Pakistanis (indigenes)

indicators.note: something found among other things lies within them, so the letters come from inside

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: An indigenous person is counted among the people of Pakistan.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: a Sindi is a native of Sind, a province of Pakistan.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sindi is a native of Sind in Pakistan, so one of that country's indigenous peoples.

clue.text: Reticent nursemaid, thoroughly contained

indicators.note: something contained is held inside, so the adverb goes within the nursemaid word

parts.note: a bonne is a French nursemaid
out means completely, as in tired out

explanation.surface: A tight-lipped nanny keeps herself completely in check.
explanation.definitionFit: Boutonné is French for buttoned up, used in English of a reserved, uncommunicative person.

clue.text: Lancaster's pierced by his first (rare) outburst

definitions.note: blurt is chiefly a verb; the setter flags its noun use with (rare), which is why a noun can define it

indicators.note: something pierced has another thing driven into it, so a letter goes inside

parts.note: Burt Lancaster was the Hollywood actor
his refers back to Lancaster, whose surname begins with L

explanation.surface: An actor makes a rare outburst, wounded by his own opening line.
explanation.walkthrough: '(rare)' marks blurt as a noun, a rare use of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A blurt is a sudden exclamation, the noun from the verb to blurt out.

clue.text: Cues if botched limit us

indicators.note: a botched job is messed up, so the letters end up out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Prompts would restrict us if they were mishandled.
explanation.definitionFit: Stimuli are things that provoke a response, and cues are signals prompting action.

clue.text: Case, note, leading to jail (6, two words)

parts.note: a theca is a sheath or case in anatomy and botany
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A legal case and a note together land someone in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks legal, but it is the biological word theca, a protective sheath.
explanation.definitionFit: The can is slang, chiefly American, for prison.

clue.text: Knitwear style ma's half unravelled

indicators.note: half of a two-letter word is just one of its letters, here the second

parts.note: the second half of ma
knitting or a stocking that has run has come unravelled

explanation.surface: Mum's half-finished jumper has come undone.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder in knitting or a stocking is called a run, so ran means came unravelled.
explanation.definitionFit: Aran is the style of thick cabled knitting from the Aran Islands off Ireland.

clue.text: Geordie's washing down third of vodka after gluttony, say

indicators.note: the vodka letter comes after the vice, fixing the order

parts.note: gluttony is one of the seven deadly sins

indicators.note: the third of a word is its third letter only

parts.note: the third letter of vodka

explanation.surface: A Geordie washes down vodka after overeating.
explanation.walkthrough: Geordie means a Tynesider; sind is a northern dialect word for rinse or wash down. 'Washing down' belongs to the definition, not to the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Sind, also sinde, is a Scots and northern English verb meaning to rinse or swill down with liquid.

clue.text: Necklace for Roman

parts.note: for and to can be interchanged, as in a toast to or for someone
RC stands for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: A necklace intended for an ancient Roman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' suggests antiquity, but it stands for a Roman Catholic, RC.
explanation.definitionFit: A torc is a rigid twisted metal neck ring worn by Celts and other ancient peoples.

clue.text: One applying pressure or trailing calamity? I'd back off

indicators.note: back means read in the opposite direction, so the two letters run right to left
trailing means following behind, so the short word comes last
taken off means removed from the calamity word

parts.note: distress is misfortune or calamity
taken as written, letters only
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone piling on pressure, or following disaster, asks to step back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'd back off' reads as a polite retreat, but it tells you to remove the reversed pair from the front of the calamity word.
explanation.definitionFit: A stressor is anything that causes stress, an agent applying strain or pressure.

clue.text: Instalment as before controls a wee bittie mixed (old)

parts.note: reins are the controls of a horse
tate is a Scots word for a small piece or lock
ment is an old past participle of meng, to mix

explanation.surface: A payment is restored as before, with someone controlling a tiny Scottish share.
explanation.walkthrough: Instalment here is the old sense of installing someone in office, not a part-payment; doing it again as before is reinstatement.
explanation.definitionFit: Instalment once meant the act of installing someone in a post, so restoring them as before is reinstatement.
